meta.blurb: Elizabeth Bennet hears a rich stranger call her barely tolerable, and she decides to dislike him for life. Mr Darcy, however, cannot stop looking at her. Two proud people, five sisters and one very wrong first impression.
meta.bible:
Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen, 1813, retold in full for learners. Voice: warm, witty, gently ironic, close to Austen; Elizabeth's view of people is quick and sometimes wrong. Place: Hertfordshire, England, about 1811 to 1812, with a spring visit to Kent and a summer tour of Derbyshire.
The Bennets of Longbourn, a village near Meryton in Hertfordshire. Mr Bennet: clever, lazy, sarcastic, loves his library; estate worth two thousand pounds a year. Mrs Bennet: silly, loud, nervous, wants all five daughters married. Daughters: Jane (about twenty-two, the beauty, gentle, sees only good in people); Elizabeth, called Lizzy (twenty, dark bright eyes, witty, her father's favourite); Mary (plain, serious, reads and plays the piano badly); Kitty (Catherine, follows Lydia); Lydia (sixteen, loud, wild, loves officers).
The Entail: Longbourn is entailed, so after Mr Bennet it passes to a male heir, the cousin Mr Collins, and the daughters will be poor.
Mrs Bennet's brother Mr Gardiner and his wife live in Gracechurch Street, London; he is in trade, they are sensible, kind and fashionable in the best way; Mrs Gardiner grew up in Lambton, Derbyshire. Mrs Bennet's sister Mrs Phillips lives in Meryton with Mr Phillips, an attorney.
Netherfield Park: the great house three miles from Longbourn. Mr Bingley: young, rich, from the north of England, four or five thousand pounds a year, cheerful, easily led, rents Netherfield. His sisters: Caroline Bingley (Miss Bingley, proud, fashionable, wants Darcy) and Louisa, Mrs Hurst, married to Mr Hurst, who likes eating and cards and is lazy.
Mr Darcy: Fitzwilliam Darcy, tall, handsome, ten thousand pounds a year, owner of Pemberley in Derbyshire; proud, shy, reserved at first; Bingley's close friend. His sister Georgiana Darcy, fifteen at the time of the old trouble, now sixteen, very shy and gifted at music. His aunt is Lady Catherine de Bourgh of Rosings Park in Kent, who has a sickly daughter, Anne de Bourgh, and wants Darcy to marry her. His cousin Colonel Fitzwilliam, an earl's younger son, about thirty, easy and agreeable.
Charlotte Lucas: Elizabeth's sensible friend, twenty-seven, plain, poor. Her father Sir William Lucas was knighted when he was mayor and lives at Lucas Lodge near Meryton with Lady Lucas; their younger daughter is Maria Lucas.
Mr Collins: William Collins, twenty-five, a clergyman, pompous and servile, rector at Hunsford in Kent through Lady Catherine; lives in the Parsonage. Hunsford Parsonage is next to Rosings Park. Mrs Jenkinson is Anne's companion.
Mr Wickham: George Wickham, handsome and charming officer in the Militia regiment stationed at Meryton, son of old Mr Wickham, the steward of Pemberley; Darcy's father was his godfather. Mr Denny: an officer, his friend. Colonel Forster: the Colonel of the Regiment; Mrs Forster is his young wife, Lydia's friend. Miss King: a girl who inherits ten thousand pounds, Wickham's brief target. Mrs Younge: Georgiana's former companion, who helped Wickham. Mr Jones: the apothecary of Meryton. Mrs Reynolds: the housekeeper at Pemberley. Mrs Nicholls: housekeeper at Netherfield.
Places: Meryton, Lucas Lodge, Longbourn, Netherfield, Hunsford, Rosings, Pemberley, Lambton, Derbyshire, Kent, London, Gracechurch Street, Cheapside, Brighton, Ramsgate, Gretna Green, Newcastle, Scotland, England. The Militia is a part-time army; the Regiment is its unit; Fordyce's Sermons is a book Collins reads aloud. The Ball at Meryton (the Assembly) and the Ball at Netherfield.
Fixed facts: Darcy first calls Elizabeth tolerable at the Meryton ball. Wickham says Darcy refused him a church living; Darcy's letter says Wickham took three thousand pounds instead, spent it, then tried to elope with Georgiana for her fortune. Darcy persuaded Bingley that Jane did not love him, and told no one he hid Jane's visit to London. Darcy first proposes at Hunsford and is refused; he proposes again at Longbourn and is accepted. Lydia marries Wickham after Darcy finds them in London and pays; Mr Bennet thinks it was Mr Gardiner. Bingley marries Jane; Elizabeth marries Darcy.

B1B2: “My dear Mr Bennet,” said his wife, “have you heard that Netherfield Park has been taken at last?” Mr Bennet had not, so she told him that a rich young man from the north of England had come to live there.

Mrs Bennet wanted her husband to visit the young man at once, so that he might marry one of their daughters. Mr Bennet only teased her, saying that she was as handsome as any of the girls and should go herself.

The Bennets had five daughters: Jane the beauty, Elizabeth the clever one, Mary the reader, and the lively Kitty and Lydia. Their father was clever and sarcastic, but their mother was a nervous woman whose only business was to find them husbands.

Mr Bennet had been among the first to visit Mr Bingley, though he had told his family nothing. When he finally said so, his daughters cried out with joy, and Mrs Bennet declared that he was the best of husbands.

Mr Bingley returned the call and sat ten minutes in the library, while the ladies watched his blue coat from a window. Then he was called away to London, and Mrs Bennet feared that he would never settle at Netherfield at all.

People said Mr Bingley would bring twelve ladies and seven gentlemen to the Meryton ball. In fact only five arrived: Mr Bingley, his two sisters, the husband of one of them, and a tall friend named Mr Darcy.

Mr Bingley was handsome, cheerful and easy in his manners, and within minutes he had made friends with half the room. He danced every dance, said that he was sorry the evening must end, and talked of giving a ball himself at Netherfield.

His friend Mr Darcy was tall and handsome, with ten thousand pounds a year, and the room admired him for half the evening. Then people saw that he was proud, that he looked down on everyone, and that nothing could please him.

Bingley danced twice with Jane, but Mr Darcy refused to dance with anyone outside his own party. When Bingley urged him to ask Elizabeth, who sat nearby, he said she was only tolerable and not handsome enough to tempt him.

Elizabeth had overheard every word, but she told the story with great spirit, because she loved anything ridiculous. At home Mrs Bennet told her husband about the ball, praised Mr Bingley's attentions to Jane, and complained loudly about Mr Darcy.

That night Jane admitted to Elizabeth how much she liked Mr Bingley, who was sensible, good-humoured and lively. Elizabeth was pleased, though she teased Jane for always thinking well of everybody and never seeing a single fault.

Mr Bingley's sisters were fine ladies from an expensive London school, and they were proud rather than kind. Their family fortune had come from trade, yet they thought themselves above the neighbours, though they agreed that Jane was a sweet girl.

Charlotte Lucas, the sensible daughter of Sir William, was Elizabeth's closest friend, and the two girls always talked over a ball together afterwards. This time Charlotte said it was no surprise that Mr Bingley admired Jane, who was by far the prettiest woman in the room.

Charlotte thought Jane should show her feelings more plainly, since a man who sees no sign of love may never try to win it. “Happiness in marriage is a matter of chance,” she said, “so a woman had better show more affection than she feels.”

When the Lucases visited Longbourn the ball was discussed again, and Mary, who liked to lecture, remarked that pride is a common failing. “I could easily forgive his pride,” said Elizabeth, “if he had not mortified mine.”

Mr Darcy had scarcely admitted that Elizabeth was pretty, but he now noticed that her dark eyes made her face unusually clever. He also saw that her figure was light and pleasing, and that her manners, though not fashionable, were playful and easy.

At a party at Lucas Lodge, Mr Darcy stood near Elizabeth and Charlotte and listened to them, though he did not mean to join in. Elizabeth whispered that she would tease him, then asked if he had not thought her very energetic when she begged for a ball.

Elizabeth was asked to play, and she sang a little and played pleasantly, though not as well as she would have liked. Mary, who had worked hard and longed for praise, sat down next and played a long concerto while the younger girls grew restless.

Sir William Lucas, who loved fine company, told Mr Darcy that dancing was one of the finest polite pleasures. Then he offered Elizabeth's hand to Darcy, who was ready to take it, but she drew it away, not wishing to dance.

Miss Bingley said she knew exactly what Mr Darcy was thinking, because he had been silent for so long. “I was thinking,” he answered, “of the pleasure that a pair of fine eyes can give, and they belong to Miss Elizabeth Bennet.”

Mr Bennet's estate of Longbourn, worth two thousand pounds a year, was entailed, so after his death it must pass to a male cousin. His wife could never speak of it without anger, because it meant that her five daughters would be left with very little.

Meryton, the little town a mile from Longbourn, was full of excitement, because a regiment of soldiers had come to stay for the winter. Kitty and Lydia walked there every morning for news, and their father called them two of the silliest girls in the country.

A note came from Miss Bingley asking Jane to dine at Netherfield with her sister, because the gentlemen were dining elsewhere. Mrs Bennet, who had seen the dark clouds, said that Jane must go on horseback, because rain would make her stay the night.

The rain fell all evening, and Jane, who had been soaked on the road, caught a bad cold and was put to bed at Netherfield. Mrs Bennet was not sorry, for she hoped that a long stay would bring Jane and Mr Bingley closer together.

Jane's note next morning said that she had a sore throat and headache, and Elizabeth could not rest until she had seen her. Since the horses were needed on the farm, she decided to walk three miles across the fields, and she set off alone.

Elizabeth reached Netherfield with muddy stockings and a glowing face, and Miss Bingley and her sister stared at her in disbelief. Mr Darcy, however, thought that the exercise had made her eyes brighter, even while he wondered whether she should have come so far alone.

Mr Jones, the apothecary, said that Jane had a fever and must not travel, so Elizabeth stayed to nurse her. Mr Bingley kindly begged her to stay, but his sisters laughed at her muddy petticoats the moment she left the room.

In the evening, when Jane was asleep, Elizabeth joined the party in the drawing room, where the others were playing cards. She chose a book instead, and Mr Darcy said that a good library should be the work of many generations.

Miss Bingley and Mr Darcy agreed that an accomplished woman must have music, singing, drawing, dancing and languages, and also a well-read mind. “I am no longer surprised that you know only six accomplished women,” said Elizabeth, “and I rather wonder that you know any.”

Mrs Bennet visited with her two youngest daughters, said Jane was too ill to move, and made Elizabeth blush with her loud talk. Lydia boldly reminded Mr Bingley that he had promised a ball, and he agreed to give one as soon as Jane was well.

Mr Darcy sat writing a letter to his sister, and Miss Bingley, who sat beside him, praised his handwriting and the length of his lines. She begged him to give her love to his sister, and he answered that he had already done so once, at her request.

Mr Bingley boasted that he could leave Netherfield in five minutes, and Elizabeth laughed that it was exactly what she expected. Mr Darcy thought that giving way too quickly showed weakness, but Elizabeth asked whether one should not yield to a friend.

That evening Jane was well enough to join the party, and Mr Bingley was so glad that he built up the fire for her. Miss Bingley, who wanted only Darcy's attention, took the book he was reading, but soon she grew bored and yawned loudly.

Miss Bingley, hoping that Mr Darcy would admire her figure, began to walk up and down the room, and invited Elizabeth to join her. Elizabeth refused, and Mr Darcy, who was asked too, said that the ladies must either be sharing secrets or wishing to show their figures.

Elizabeth said she would love to laugh at Mr Darcy, but she hoped she never mocked what was wise or good. Follies and whims amused her, she said, and Darcy answered that it had been the study of his life to avoid such weaknesses.

“I cannot forget other people's faults as quickly as I should,” said Darcy, “and my good opinion, once lost, is lost for ever.” “That is a failing indeed,” said Elizabeth, “but I cannot laugh at it, for you have chosen your fault well.”

While Miss Bingley played a lively Scottish tune, Mr Darcy asked Elizabeth whether she felt inclined to dance a reel. “You hoped I would say yes, so you could despise me,” she said, “but I say no, so despise me if you dare.”

Mr Darcy realised that he was in some danger of admiring Elizabeth too much, and that only her inferior family kept him safe. Miss Bingley, who saw his look, grew jealous and mocked the Bennets' relations, hoping to cure him of any liking for Elizabeth.

Elizabeth wrote to her mother asking for the carriage, but Mrs Bennet replied that it could not be sent before Tuesday. The sisters then asked for Mr Bingley's carriage, but he begged them to stay, so they agreed to leave on Sunday.

On Sunday morning Jane and Elizabeth said goodbye, and Miss Bingley's thanks were warm, because she was glad to see Elizabeth go. At Longbourn their father welcomed them gladly, but their mother grumbled that they had come home too early.
At dinner Mr Bennet said that he had a letter from his cousin Mr Collins, who would one day inherit Longbourn. He promised to read it aloud, since it was bound to be amusing.

Mr Collins wrote that he was a clergyman, and that his patroness, Lady Catherine de Bourgh, had given him a church in Kent. He hoped to end an old family quarrel and asked if he might visit the Bennets for a week.

Mr Collins arrived at four o'clock, a tall, heavy young man of twenty-five with a serious air and very formal manners. He admired the house and praised the dinner so warmly that Mrs Bennet replied rather sharply that they could afford a good cook.

Mr Collins spoke proudly of Lady Catherine de Bourgh, and of her daughter, who he said was born to be a duchess. Mr Bennet, enjoying every word, asked whether such fine compliments were planned or came to him at the moment.

After tea Mr Collins offered to read aloud to the ladies, and he took down a volume of Fordyce's sermons. Lydia stopped him after three pages by chattering about the officers at Meryton, so he turned, offended, to backgammon with Mr Bennet.

Mr Collins had come to Longbourn with a plan: he meant to choose a wife from among his cousins, as a kind of peace offering. He thought of Jane first, but Mrs Bennet hinted that she might soon be engaged, so he chose Elizabeth, who came next in age.

The next morning the girls walked to Meryton with Mr Collins, and in the street they met Mr Denny, an officer, with a stranger. The stranger, Mr Wickham, had a fine figure, a handsome face and such pleasing manners that all the girls looked at him.
As they talked, Mr Bingley and Mr Darcy rode up, and Bingley bowed to Jane, who blushed with pleasure. Then Darcy saw Mr Wickham, and both men changed colour: one turned white and the other red.

Elizabeth saw it all, and she wondered what could have caused such a strange meeting between two gentlemen. Mr Denny said that Mr Wickham was to join the regiment, and the girls hurried to Mrs Phillips's house to talk about him.

Mrs Phillips invited the whole family to supper the next evening, promising that Mr Wickham would come with the other officers. Mr Collins wondered whether a party suited a clergyman, but Mr Bennet assured him that one quiet evening would do no harm.

Mr Collins looked round Mrs Phillips's drawing room and declared that it was almost as fine as a small room at Rosings. The officers arrived, and Mr Wickham, who was by far the handsomest, walked in last and took the seat beside Elizabeth.

While the others played cards for fish, Mr Wickham talked pleasantly to Elizabeth, first of the rain and then of the neighbourhood. At last he asked, rather carefully, how long Mr Darcy had been staying at Netherfield.

Mr Wickham explained that his father had been steward of the Pemberley estate, and that Mr Darcy's father had been his godfather. The old gentleman, he said, had loved him like a son and had meant to look after him for life.

Wickham said that the old Mr Darcy had promised him a good position in the church, which he hoped to hold one day. But when the old man died and the place became free, the new master gave it to another man.

“He deserves to be disgraced before the world,” cried Elizabeth, “for such cruelty to a friend!” Wickham replied that he would never expose the son of his old master, though he felt the unfairness deeply.

Wickham added that Darcy's pride made him generous to his tenants and the poor, and a careful brother to his sister. He also said that Lady Catherine hoped Darcy would marry her daughter, and Elizabeth smiled to think of Miss Bingley's wasted efforts.

The next morning Elizabeth told Jane everything that Wickham had said, and Jane listened with growing distress. She could not believe that Mr Bingley's friend could be so cruel, and she felt sure that there was some mistake.

For about half the evening the gentlemen pronounced him a fine figure of a man and the ladies declared him handsomer than Mr Bingley. But his manners soon turned the tide, for he was discovered to think himself far above the company and impossible to please, and not even his great estate in Derbyshire could save him from being thought disagreeable.

Mr Bingley danced twice with Jane Bennet, the loveliest girl in the room, and was plainly delighted with her, while Mr Darcy danced only with the ladies of his own party and walked about looking bored. Pressed by his friend to ask Elizabeth Bennet, who sat close by for want of a partner, he glanced at her for a moment and then coldly withdrew his eyes. “She is tolerable,” he said, “but not handsome enough to tempt me, and I am in no humour to give consequence to young ladies whom other men have slighted.”

Elizabeth had heard every word, and instead of being wounded she told the story afterwards to all her friends with great spirit, for she had a playful, lively disposition and delighted in anything ridiculous. At Longbourn, meanwhile, Mrs Bennet gave her husband an account of the evening, praising Mr Bingley's attentions to Jane, who had been so much admired, and then fell to complaining of the dreadful rudeness of Mr Darcy. “He is a most disagreeable, horrid man,” she cried, “and not at all worth pleasing, and I wish you had been there to give him one of your set-downs!”

That night, when she was alone with Elizabeth, Jane confessed with glowing cheeks how much she admired Mr Bingley, whose manners were so pleasing and whose temper was so good. Elizabeth, delighted but unable to resist a joke, said that he was handsome, as a young man ought to be, and that Jane, who had never seen a fault in anyone, was the worst judge in the world. “You are too ready to like people in general,” she added, “and I am afraid you will end by liking everybody.”

Mr Bingley's sisters were fashionable ladies, educated at one of the best schools in London, with a fortune of twenty thousand pounds each and a firm belief in their own superiority. Their family had made its money in trade, a fact they preferred to forget, and they hoped to marry into families of higher rank. They found the ladies of Meryton rather coarse, and yet they agreed, with some condescension, that Jane was a sweet girl whom they would not object to know better.

Charlotte Lucas, the sensible and rather plain daughter of Sir William Lucas, was Elizabeth's closest friend, and the two girls always talked over a ball together once the candles had been put out. The Lucases lived at Lucas Lodge, a short walk from Longbourn, in a house that Sir William, who had once been a tradesman and was now a knight, loved to fill with company. Charlotte, who was twenty-seven and had no fortune, observed that Mr Bingley's liking for Jane was no surprise, since he had danced with her twice and she was by far the prettiest woman in the room.

Charlotte had a clear, practical view of such matters, and she warned Elizabeth that Jane was too calm and cheerful to be understood by a man who knew her so little. If a woman conceals her affection, she said, she may lose the chance of securing him, and there is generally more gratitude and vanity in love than people care to admit. “Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance,” she concluded, “and it is better to know as little as possible of the faults of the person with whom you are to spend your life.”

When the Lucases came to Longbourn the ball was discussed again, and Mrs Bennet listed every one of Mr Darcy's offences, while Mary, who liked to lecture, observed that pride is a very common failing. “If I were as rich as Mr Darcy,” cried the youngest Lucas boy, “I would keep a pack of hounds and drink a bottle of wine every day, and I should not care how proud I was!” Elizabeth, who had been silent for some time, said lightly that she could easily forgive his pride if he had not mortified hers.

Mr Darcy had scarcely allowed himself to admit that Elizabeth Bennet was pretty, and he had looked at her at the ball only to find fault. But no sooner had he decided that her features were not good than he noticed that her dark eyes gave her face a rare intelligence. He found, too, that her figure was light and pleasing, and that her manners, though not those of the fashionable world, had a playful ease that captured his attention against his will.

At a party at Lucas Lodge, Mr Darcy stood near enough to Elizabeth and Charlotte to overhear their talk, though he gave no sign that he meant to join in. Elizabeth, who guessed that he was listening, whispered to her friend that she was determined to tease him, and then asked whether he had not thought her very energetic just now, when she was begging for a ball at Meryton. He replied with great gravity that she had spoken with much energy, but that the subject always made a lady energetic, and Elizabeth, hoping for a livelier answer, laughed.

Elizabeth was soon asked to play, and she sang a little and played pleasantly, though neither so well nor so carefully as she could have wished. Mary, who had worked hard at her accomplishments and longed for praise, sat down at the piano after her and played a long concerto in a manner that was learned rather than lovely. The younger Bennets and some of the Lucases, impatient to dance, had begun to form a set at the other end of the room, while Mr Darcy stood by in silent indignation at an evening without conversation.

Sir William Lucas, who thought that being knighted was a fine thing and dancing a finer, told Mr Darcy that nothing was so delightful as a dance among polite young people. Darcy answered with a slight bow that dancing had the advantage of being popular among the less polished societies of the world, for every savage can dance. When Sir William took Elizabeth's hand to offer it to Darcy, who was by no means unwilling, she drew it back and said, a little confused, that she had not the least wish to dance.

Miss Bingley, who watched Mr Darcy's every look with an attention that she believed she hid, observed that she could guess exactly what he was thinking, because he had been silent for a long time. Darcy, startled and amused, replied that he had been thinking of the pleasure that a pair of fine eyes can give a woman's face, and when she asked whose, he said at once that they were Miss Elizabeth Bennet's. Miss Bingley, astonished and a little alarmed, began to congratulate him in a mocking voice, and to describe what a delightful mother-in-law Mrs Bennet would make.

Mr Bennet's property consisted almost wholly of the estate of Longbourn, which brought in two thousand pounds a year and which was, unfortunately for his daughters, entailed on a distant male cousin. Mrs Bennet's own fortune, which had come from her father, an attorney in Meryton, was only four thousand pounds, and it could never make up for the loss of the estate that her daughters would suffer. She could never hear the word entail without a storm of nerves, and she complained so bitterly that Mr Bennet had taken to shutting himself in his library.

Meryton, the little market town a mile from Longbourn, was now the centre of the girls' universe, for a regiment of the militia had arrived to spend the winter there, and the streets were full of scarlet coats. Mrs Phillips, Mrs Bennet's sister, who lived in the town with her attorney husband, supplied the name, family and rank of every officer, and Kitty and Lydia walked in each morning to hear it. Their father observed drily that they must be two of the silliest girls in the country, a suspicion he had long held and that each day confirmed.

A note came for Jane from Miss Bingley, inviting her to dine that evening at Netherfield with her sister, while the gentlemen of the house dined elsewhere with the officers. Mrs Bennet, who had already noticed the black clouds, declared that Jane must go on horseback, because it was sure to rain and she would then be obliged to stay all night. Jane, who knew her mother's schemes only too well, set off on the horse with a mixture of doubt and obedience.

The rain came down in torrents all evening, and Jane did not return, which Mrs Bennet greeted with open delight as a proof of her own cleverness. But the next morning a note arrived in Jane's own hand, written with a shaking pen, to say that she had been soaked on the road and had been put to bed at Netherfield with a bad cold. Mr Bennet remarked that if his daughter were to die, it would be a comfort to know that it had all been done in pursuit of Mr Bingley and under his wife's orders.

Elizabeth, who could not be easy about her sister, resolved to go to her, and since the carriage was not to be had and she was no horsewoman, she announced that she would walk the three miles. Her mother protested that she would be splashed to the knees, and Mr Bennet merely observed that the horses were wanted on the farm, while Kitty and Lydia offered to go with her as far as Meryton. She crossed field after field at a quick pace, springing over stiles and jumping puddles, with anxiety in her heart and mud on her stockings, and arrived at last with her face glowing from the exercise.

The ladies of Netherfield were at breakfast when Elizabeth was shown in, and Miss Bingley and Mrs Hurst stared with horror at a young woman who had walked three miles in such weather, with her petticoats deep in mud. Mr Bingley received her warmly, and Mr Darcy, who said very little, was divided between admiration for the colour the exercise had given her and doubt whether so long a walk alone was proper. Mr Hurst, who cared for nothing in the world but his breakfast, said not a word, and Miss Bingley whispered to her sister that such an arrival was beyond belief.

Mr Jones, the apothecary, was sent for, and he pronounced that Miss Bennet had caught a violent cold and a fever, and that she must on no account be moved. Mr Bingley begged Elizabeth to remain and nurse her sister, and he sent at once to Longbourn for her clothes, while his sisters, who could hardly refuse, were civil to her face. The moment she had left the room, however, they began to laugh at her muddy petticoats and her wild hair, and to wonder at a girl who would walk three miles for the sake of a sister's cold.

In the evening, when Jane was asleep, Elizabeth went down to the drawing room, where the party had settled to cards, and refused to join them, saying that she would rather read. Mr Bingley offered to fetch any book his library contained, and regretted that it was so small, for he was an idle fellow who had never read half of what he owned. Mr Darcy said that a good library must be the work of many generations, and Miss Bingley, who hung on his every word, praised the library at Pemberley with a fervour she had never felt for any book.

Miss Bingley declared that no woman could be called accomplished without music, singing, drawing, dancing and languages, and Mr Darcy added that she must also improve her mind by extensive reading. Elizabeth, who had listened in silence, replied that she was no longer surprised that he knew only six accomplished women, and that she rather wondered at his knowing any. Miss Bingley, who thought that she possessed every one of these gifts, protested that she knew many such women, and the conversation ended in a politeness that was cooler than before.

Mrs Bennet arrived at Netherfield next morning with Kitty and Lydia, and, after hearing from the apothecary that Jane was far too ill to be moved, she thanked Mr Bingley loudly for his kindness. Elizabeth, in a quiet agony of shame, wished the carpet would open beneath her while her mother boasted of her daughters and made foolish remarks about the country. Lydia, a stout, bold girl of fifteen, reminded Mr Bingley of his promise to give a ball at Netherfield, and he declared that he would hold it as soon as her sister was well.

The next morning Mr Darcy sat writing to his sister Georgiana, while Miss Bingley, who had placed herself at his elbow, interrupted him every few moments to praise his handwriting and the astonishing length of his letter. She begged him to tell his sister how much she longed to see her, and he replied, without lifting his eyes, that he had already told her so once at Miss Bingley's own request. Elizabeth, sitting nearby with her needlework, watched the whole performance with silent amusement and drew her own conclusions about the lady's hopes.

Mr Bingley, who was easy and careless, boasted that if he ever resolved to leave Netherfield he would be gone in five minutes, and Elizabeth said that this was exactly what she would have expected of him. Mr Darcy answered that it showed less an easy temper than a weak one, since a man who yields at once to any friend's request does not trouble to examine the reasons. Elizabeth replied that she saw no great virtue in a friendship that demanded reasons before every favour, and that a friend might surely be persuaded without being given an argument.

By the evening Jane was well enough to join the party, and Mr Bingley was so delighted that he built up the fire and hardly left her side for the rest of the night. Miss Bingley, whose whole attention was fixed on Mr Darcy, took up the second volume of his book to show that she shared his interests, but she soon gave a loud yawn and declared that there was nothing like reading. Her pretence deceived nobody, and Mr Darcy, who did not so much as lift his head, turned a page with perfect composure.

Miss Bingley, who was determined to be noticed, began to walk about the room, for her figure was elegant and she walked well, and she invited Elizabeth to join her. Elizabeth declined with surprise, but Miss Bingley, still unsuccessful, begged Mr Darcy to join them, and he looked up from his book at last. “If you are sharing secrets, I should be in your way,” he said, “and if you wish to show your figures, I can admire you far better from the fire.”

Elizabeth cried that they must tease him for such a speech, and Miss Bingley, who thought it impossible to laugh at Mr Darcy, said that she knew of no one so impervious. “I should like to find some folly in him to laugh at,” said Elizabeth, “but I hope I never ridicule what is wise or good, though nonsense and whims and inconsistencies amuse me.” Darcy replied that perhaps nobody could escape ridicule altogether, but that it had been the study of his life to avoid the weaknesses that expose a strong understanding to mockery.

Darcy said, in his stern way, that his temper was perhaps resentful, since he could not forget the follies of others as soon as he ought, and that his good opinion, once lost, was lost for ever. “That is a failing indeed,” cried Elizabeth, “and I cannot laugh at it, for you have chosen your fault well, but I think you have a tendency to hate everybody.” “And yours,” he replied with a smile, “is wilfully to misunderstand everyone, and I will not argue the point.”

While Miss Bingley, tired of Darcy's silence, played a lively Scottish air on the piano, Mr Darcy came to Elizabeth's side and asked whether she did not feel a great inclination to dance a reel. She smiled and did not answer, and when he repeated the question with some surprise, she said that she had heard him perfectly well but had needed a moment to decide what to say. “You wanted me to say yes, so that you might despise me,” she said, “but I delight in overthrowing such schemes, so I will not dance at all, and now despise me if you dare.”

Darcy, who had expected a blush of gratified vanity, was astonished and delighted by her answer, and he felt that if her relations had been less inferior he should have been in danger of admiring her too much. Miss Bingley, whose jealousy had been fed by every glance he gave Elizabeth, began to speak of the Bennets' uncle the attorney at Meryton and the uncle in trade in London, hoping to cure him of his liking. Darcy listened with studied calm, asked whether she had anything more to propose for his domestic happiness, and was soon left in peace to reflect upon the danger.

Elizabeth, anxious to be gone, wrote to her mother to beg for the carriage in the morning, but Mrs Bennet replied that it could not be spared before Tuesday. The sisters then asked Mr Bingley for the loan of his own carriage, but he begged them so kindly to stay that they agreed to leave on Sunday instead. Mr Darcy, who was glad and sorry at once, resolved to show Elizabeth no more attention than good manners demanded, lest he should betray what he was beginning to feel.

On Sunday morning Jane and Elizabeth took their leave, and Miss Bingley's thanks were warm and her curtsey low, for she was never so civil as when she was glad to be rid of a guest. Mr Darcy bade Elizabeth a distant, careful farewell, and she, who had noticed his coolness and not understood it, put it down to his habitual pride. At Longbourn their father welcomed them gladly, for the evening conversation had been much less lively without them, but their mother grumbled that Jane had been brought home too soon.

At dinner Mr Bennet announced, with a gleam in his eye, that he had received a letter from his cousin Mr Collins, the young man who would one day turn them all out of the house. Mrs Bennet, who could not bear the name, protested that it was the hardest thing in the world that his estate should be entailed away from his own children. Mr Bennet, undisturbed, promised to read the letter aloud after dinner, adding that he had great hopes of finding the writer a very foolish man.

The letter, which was long, pompous and very correct, explained that Mr Collins was a clergyman, and that his patroness, Lady Catherine de Bourgh, had given him a comfortable church in Kent. He wrote that he was sorry to be the means of injuring such amiable young ladies, and that he hoped to end the old quarrel between his late father and Mr Bennet. He proposed to visit on Monday and to stay for a week, and Mr Bennet, folding up the letter, remarked that there was something promising in a man who wrote so well and so foolishly.

Mr Collins arrived punctually at four o'clock, a tall, heavy-looking young man of five-and-twenty, with a grave and stately air and manners that were extremely formal. He had hardly sat down when he complimented Mrs Bennet on her fine daughters, saying that he had heard much of their beauty but that fame had fallen short of the truth. At dinner he admired the furniture and the meal so warmly that he asked which of his fair cousins had cooked it, until Mrs Bennet replied sharply that they could afford a good cook.

Mr Collins spoke of nothing so willingly as Lady Catherine de Bourgh, whose kindness, he said, had no equal, for she had visited his humble home and had even condescended to approve his arrangements. He described her only daughter, Miss de Bourgh, as a delicate young lady who seemed born to be a duchess, though her weak health had kept her from many accomplishments. Mr Bennet, who was enjoying himself greatly, asked whether such happy compliments were planned beforehand or came to him on the moment, and Mr Collins admitted that he sometimes prepared a few.

After tea Mr Collins was asked to read aloud to the ladies, and he fetched a volume of sermons by Fordyce, a book so solemn that Lydia stared at it in alarm. Before he had read three pages Lydia interrupted him with a breathless account of the officers at Meryton, and her mother and sisters, mortified, tried in vain to silence her. Mr Collins, deeply offended, put away the sermons, remarked that young girls care little for serious books, and sat down to play backgammon with Mr Bennet, who accepted with cheerful readiness.

Mr Collins had come to Longbourn for more than the healing of a quarrel, for he meant to choose a wife from among his cousins, as the best amends for the loss they must suffer by the entail. Lady Catherine herself, he believed, wished him to marry, and he decided that one of the Bennet girls would answer very well. He fixed first upon Jane, but Mrs Bennet hinted that she was likely to be engaged, so he chose Elizabeth, who came next in age and beauty.

The next morning Mr Collins walked to Meryton with the girls, and they had not gone far when they met Mr Denny, an officer whom Lydia knew, with a young man who was a stranger to them all. The stranger, whose name was Mr Wickham, had agreed to join the regiment, and he was so handsome, with a fine figure, a charming face and agreeable manners, that every lady looked at him with admiration. He bowed, and Elizabeth thought that she had seldom seen a man who seemed to carry so much good humour in his look.

While they were still talking, the sound of horses made them turn, and Mr Bingley and Mr Darcy came riding down the street. Bingley, who had been on his way to ask after Miss Bennet, bowed and spoke warmly to Jane, who blushed with pleasure, and he was about to ride on when Darcy's eye fell on Mr Wickham. Elizabeth, who saw it all, was struck by the change of colour in both men, one turning white and the other red, before Mr Wickham touched his hat and Darcy barely returned the bow.

Elizabeth could not imagine what the meeting meant, for she was sure that no ordinary dislike would make two gentlemen change colour in a public street. Mr Denny, when the riders were gone, said carelessly that Mr Wickham was to receive a commission in the regiment, and that he had already begun to be liked. The girls, who were far too curious to walk on, hurried to Mrs Phillips's window and spent half an hour waving to the officers, until Mr Collins, who had been staring at the shop windows, called them away.

Mrs Phillips, Mrs Bennet's sister, was delighted to see the girls, and she begged the whole family to come to supper the next evening, promising that Mr Wickham and several officers would be there. Mr Collins, who feared that a party might not suit a clergyman, was assured by Mr Bennet that one evening of cards would do him no harm, and he accepted at once. Kitty and Lydia talked of nothing else all the way home, while Elizabeth, who said little, kept returning in her thoughts to the strange look that had passed between Mr Wickham and Mr Darcy.

Mr Collins was so struck by the size and furniture of Mrs Phillips's drawing room that he declared he might have supposed himself in the small summer breakfast parlour at Rosings. Mrs Phillips, who had never heard of Rosings until it was explained to her, was flattered and listened to his account of Lady Catherine's chimney-piece with the greatest respect. When the officers entered, Mr Wickham, who was far above the rest in person, air and walk, came in last, and he took the chair beside Elizabeth with a smile that she could not help returning.

The others settled to cards, and Mr Collins sat down to whist with great pleasure, but Elizabeth, who did not care to play, was glad to find her chair a delightful place to listen. Mr Wickham talked to her of the weather, the wet season and the regiment, and he told it with such grace that even the most ordinary subject became interesting. After a time he asked, with some hesitation, how long Mr Darcy had been at Netherfield, and when she said it was nearly a month, he remarked that nobody knew him better.

Wickham told her, in a low and feeling voice, that his own father had been the steward of the great estate of Pemberley, and that the late Mr Darcy, the best man who ever lived, had been his godfather. The old gentleman had loved him like a son, he said, had sent him to school and to the university, and had meant to provide for him all his life. He spoke of a gratitude he could never repay, and of the young Mr Darcy, who, although they had played together as boys, had never been able to bear his place in his father's affection.

He had expected, he said, to be given the best church living in the family's gift as soon as it fell vacant, for the old man had meant him to become a clergyman. But when the old man died and the place did fall vacant, the young Mr Darcy, who could not endure him, gave it to another. “It was not a matter that the law could mend, for the promise was only a wish,” he said quietly, “but I cannot think that I deserved such a loss.”

“This is quite shocking,” cried Elizabeth, whose cheeks were burning, “and he deserves to be disgraced before the whole world!” Wickham answered that some time or other he would be, but that it should not be by him, for he could never defy or expose the son of the man he had loved. Elizabeth, who thought him more handsome for his forbearance, said that she had never imagined Mr Darcy capable of such malicious revenge, such injustice and such inhumanity.

Wickham went on, with an air of fairness that did him credit, to say that Darcy's pride had often made him generous, for he helped his tenants, relieved the poor and was a careful guardian to his sister. This was family pride, he said, and pride in what his father had been, and it made Darcy unwilling to disgrace his name or to lose the good opinion of his friends. He added that Lady Catherine hoped her daughter would marry Darcy and unite two great estates, and Elizabeth, smiling at the thought of Miss Bingley's wasted efforts, trusted him the more for his frankness.

The next morning Elizabeth told Jane everything that Mr Wickham had said, and Jane, who was astonished and concerned, heard her with growing distress. She could not believe that Mr Bingley's friend could be so cruel, and yet she could not doubt Mr Wickham's honest face, so she begged her sister to believe that there had been some mistake. “They have both been deceived in some way,” said Jane, “and I would rather think that than think ill of either of them.”

A few days later a card arrived from Netherfield inviting the family to a ball on the following Tuesday, and the news drove every other subject from the minds of the household. Mrs Bennet, who read it three times aloud, declared that it was a particular compliment to Jane, and Kitty and Lydia, who were beside themselves, talked of ribbons and partners until their father begged for silence. Elizabeth was glad of the ball for her own reasons, for she hoped to dance with Mr Wickham and to watch at close hand how Mr Darcy behaved towards him.

Mr Collins accepted the invitation without scruple, saying that a ball given by so respectable a young man could do no harm to a clergyman, and then astonished Elizabeth by engaging her for the first two dances. She had hoped to dance them with Mr Wickham, but she could hardly refuse her cousin, and she gave her hand with less pleasure than he seemed to expect. It crossed her mind, with a pang of dismay, that she was being singled out as the future lady of Hunsford, and that her mother would be delighted.

Rain fell for days without ceasing, so that the younger girls could not walk to Meryton even once, and Kitty and Lydia, deprived of news, could think of nothing but the officers and the ball. Elizabeth, for her part, dressed on the evening with unusual care, choosing her ribbons as if each one mattered, for she was determined to enjoy herself. When the carriage turned into the drive at Netherfield, her eyes were already searching the line of red coats for the one she wished to see.

The ball at Netherfield was as brilliant as the neighbourhood had hoped, with candles in every room and a crowd of officers, but Elizabeth looked in vain for Mr Wickham and felt the evening lose half its charm. Mr Denny, when she asked, said that business had called Wickham to town, and added in a low voice that he did not think his friend would have gone if he had not wished to avoid a certain gentleman. Elizabeth, who had little doubt of his meaning, laid all the blame at Darcy's door, and felt so little disposed to be amused that she took her place for the dances with a heavy heart.

Elizabeth danced the first two dances with Mr Collins, and she remembered them for the rest of her life as an hour of pure misery. Mr Collins was awkward and solemn, apologised when he should have been attending, went wrong without being aware of it, and gave her all the shame and distress that a bad partner can give. The moment of her release from him was one of such relief that she could hardly speak for the pleasure of it.

Elizabeth was still lamenting her fate to Charlotte Lucas when Mr Darcy came up and asked for the pleasure of the next dance, and, taken by surprise, she accepted him before she knew what she was doing. He walked away again, leaving her to reflect with some vexation on her own want of presence of mind. “Heaven forbid,” cried Elizabeth, when Charlotte whispered that she might find him very pleasant, “for it would be the greatest misfortune of all to find agreeable a man whom one is determined to hate.”

They took their places in the set and danced for some time in perfect silence, until Elizabeth, who thought it would be a worse punishment for him to talk than to be quiet, resolved to make him speak. She made a slight remark upon the dance, to which he replied and fell silent again, and after a pause of some minutes she spoke a second time. “It is your turn to say something now, Mr Darcy,” she said, “for I have talked about the dance, and you ought to remark on the size of the room.”

He smiled and said that he would say whatever she wished, and the talk drifted for a time to books, where they found that their tastes differed, and then to Meryton and its society. At last Elizabeth, whose thoughts were with a certain absent officer, remarked that Mr Wickham had been so unlucky as to lose Mr Darcy's friendship, and in a manner that would make him suffer all his life. Darcy coloured and replied stiffly that Mr Wickham was blessed with such happy manners that he easily made friends, though whether he could keep them was less certain.

Sir William Lucas, passing close by, stopped to compliment them both on such a display of talent, and added, with a significant glance at Jane and Mr Bingley, that he expected to see a very happy event before long. Darcy, who had been looking at Elizabeth, turned his eyes at once toward the other couple, and his face grew so thoughtful that he seemed hardly to hear the questions she asked him. Later she asked whether he was careful never to let resentment be created, and she confessed that she heard such different accounts of him that she could not make out his character.

When the dance was over, Miss Bingley, who had been watching them with sharp eyes, came to her side with a smile that was meant to look friendly. “So, Miss Eliza,” she said, “I hear that you are delighted with George Wickham, but he is only a steward's son, and Mr Darcy has treated him far better than he deserves.” Elizabeth answered coldly that she would not be moved by so paltry an attack, and she turned to Jane, who said that Bingley knew little of the quarrel but was sure of his friend's honour.

Elizabeth then saw, with great alarm, that Mr Collins, having learned that Mr Darcy was the nephew of Lady Catherine de Bourgh, was making his way towards him with the clear intention of introducing himself. She begged him not to, since it was an impertinence to speak first to a gentleman so far above him, but Mr Collins replied that the rules of the church were higher than those of the world. Darcy heard the long and flowery speech with cold astonishment, bowed slightly, and walked away, while Elizabeth, who had heard every word, felt such shame for her cousin that she could hardly lift her eyes.

At supper Elizabeth had the misfortune to sit near her mother, who was telling Lady Lucas, at the top of her voice, that she expected Jane to be married to Mr Bingley very soon. She dwelt on the match with delight, calling Mr Bingley charming, rich and handsome and saying how fond his sisters were of Jane, while Mr Darcy, a few seats away, heard every word. Elizabeth begged her to lower her voice, but Mrs Bennet answered that she did not see what Mr Darcy was to her and that she would say whatever she pleased.

After supper Mary, who had been listening to praise of her sisters, sat down at the piano and sang for so long that the guests grew weary, though the longer she sang the better pleased she was. Elizabeth, in an agony of embarrassment, looked at her father, who understood her at last and remarked aloud that Mary had delighted them quite enough and should let the other young ladies have a turn. It seemed to Elizabeth that her family had made it their business to expose themselves as much as possible, and she saw that Mr Darcy and the Bingley sisters watched it all in a silence worse than laughter.

The morning after the ball Mr Collins, who had not wasted a moment, asked Mrs Bennet whether he might have the honour of a private interview with her fair daughter Elizabeth. Mrs Bennet, who had guessed his purpose and could hardly contain her joy, replied that nothing could please her more, and she hurried the younger girls out of the room. Elizabeth, who saw what was coming, begged her mother and Kitty not to leave her, but Mrs Bennet told her not to be silly and shut the door behind them.

Mr Collins began with great solemnity by saying that he had three reasons for marrying: a clergyman should set an example, it would add to his happiness, and his noble patroness had advised it. Lady Catherine, he told her, had said that he must choose an active, useful woman who could make a small income go a long way. Since he must one day inherit Longbourn, he added, he had resolved to choose a wife among his cousins, and he cared nothing for her fortune.

Elizabeth, who was struggling not to laugh, interrupted him at last, saying that he was too hasty, since he had forgotten that she had given no answer. She thanked him for the honour of his proposal, but said that it was impossible for her to do anything but decline it. Mr Collins waved his hand and said that it was usual for young ladies to refuse the man they secretly meant to accept, and that he was by no means discouraged.

“I am perfectly serious in my refusal,” said Elizabeth, with some warmth, “and you could not make me happy, and I am convinced that I am the last woman in the world who could make you so.” She begged him to think of her not as an elegant female who wished to plague him, but as a rational creature speaking the truth from her heart. Mr Collins, who insisted that she was only being modest, declared that she was uniformly charming and that he would speak to her parents, and Elizabeth, in despair, left the room.

Mrs Bennet, who had been hovering outside the door, burst in at once, and when she learned that Elizabeth had refused she cried that the girl must marry him or never be spoken to again. She hurried to the library, where Mr Bennet sat with his book, and demanded that he command Elizabeth to accept her cousin at once. Mr Bennet, who had sent for Elizabeth, told her calmly that her mother would never see her again if she refused Mr Collins, and that he would never see her again if she accepted.

Mr Collins, who was more offended in his pride than in his heart, spent the rest of the day in cold and dignified silence, treating Elizabeth with a politeness that was worse than anger. Charlotte Lucas, who came that morning to visit, listened to his complaints with so much patience and sympathy that Elizabeth felt a real gratitude, though she did not suspect the purpose behind her kindness. Mrs Bennet, meanwhile, went from room to room lamenting her daughter's folly, and the house was so full of gloom that Mr Bennet retreated to his library.

Mr Wickham, who had been away for some days, returned to Meryton and walked out with Elizabeth and Kitty, who were on their way to see Mrs Phillips. When Elizabeth asked why he had missed the Netherfield ball, he answered that he had thought it best to avoid Mr Darcy, since he did not trust himself to meet him with composure. Elizabeth, flattered by his confidence and moved by his gentleness, thought him more agreeable than ever, and listened with an interest that made her forget everything else.

Not long afterwards a letter reached Jane from Miss Bingley, written in a neat and flowing hand, which told her that the whole party had left Netherfield for London and had no thought of returning that winter. Jane read it aloud with a face that grew paler, for although it spoke of her warmly and recalled their happy hours together, it said that the ladies were anxious to join Mr Darcy's sister. The letter ended with a hint, kind in manner and cruel in meaning, that Mr Bingley admired Miss Darcy so much that he would soon be glad to call her his own.

Jane tried to hide her grief and to persuade herself that the letter meant nothing unkind, but Elizabeth, who saw through every smooth phrase, felt sure that Miss Bingley wished to keep her brother from Jane. She told Jane, as steadily as she could, that Bingley loved her and would certainly return, and that his sisters could not govern his heart for ever. Jane, who could not quite believe it, answered that she would try to be easy and would not give way to useless tears, and the sisters spoke of it no more.

Charlotte Lucas, who made herself pleasant to Mr Collins on every occasion, was rewarded the next day, when he proposed to her at Lucas Lodge and she accepted him. When she told Elizabeth, her friend cried out that it was impossible, and Charlotte, who coloured but kept her composure, said that she was not romantic and asked only for a comfortable home. Elizabeth, struck dumb with surprise, saw that her friend had sacrificed every finer feeling to worldly advantage, and she knew that nothing between them could be quite the same again.

Sir William Lucas came to Longbourn to announce his daughter's engagement, with so many bows and so much self-satisfaction that Mrs Bennet, who was not listening, declared that he must be mistaken. When she was at last persuaded, she answered with open fury, calling Charlotte a sly creature and Mr Collins a fool, and for weeks she could not meet Lady Lucas without a quarrel. She blamed Elizabeth for the whole affair, and she was so unfriendly for so long that even Mr Bennet, who had hoped to be amused, grew weary of her complaints.

Jane, who had written to Miss Bingley at once and waited every day for a warm reply, saw the weeks pass without any word that Mr Bingley meant to return to Netherfield. Mr Bennet, who had noticed Jane's pale face, remarked to Elizabeth that, next to being married, a girl likes to be crossed in love now and then, since it gives her a sort of distinction. He added that Meryton had officers enough to disappoint every young lady in the country, and that Wickham, a pleasant fellow, would jilt her creditably.

Mr Wickham was careful to spend every evening that he could in Elizabeth's company, and his story of Mr Darcy's injustice, which he told with an air of reluctance, soon spread through Meryton. Nearly everybody agreed that Darcy was a cruel, proud and unforgiving man, and even those who had once admired his fortune began to discover that they had always disliked him. Elizabeth, who believed that she was merely sorry for an injured man, found that her sympathy had grown warmer, and that she looked for him across every room with unusual eagerness.

At Christmas Mr and Mrs Gardiner arrived at Longbourn with their four young children, and the house, which had been so long gloomy, grew lively at once. Mr Gardiner was a sensible, gentlemanlike man, far superior to his sister, and the ladies of Netherfield would have found it hard to believe that a man who lived by trade could be so well bred. Mrs Gardiner, who was several years younger than Mrs Bennet, was an amiable, intelligent and elegant woman, and she was a great favourite with Jane and Elizabeth, who had often stayed with her in town.

The Gardiners' first business was to distribute their presents and the news of London fashions, and their second was to hear Mrs Bennet's account of her wrongs, which she gave at great length. Mrs Gardiner, who listened with polite patience, was soon told by Elizabeth in private of Jane's disappointment, and her sympathy was so warm that she proposed a remedy at once. She invited Jane to return with them to London, hoping that a change of scene would revive her spirits, though Gracechurch Street was far from the fashionable streets where Mr Bingley's family lived.

Mrs Gardiner, who was too kind to be unobservant, watched Elizabeth and Mr Wickham together, and she saw that her niece was in some danger of liking him more than was prudent. She took Elizabeth aside and said gently that she was too sensible to fall in love merely because she was warned, but that she must not form an affection that want of fortune would make imprudent. Elizabeth promised to be careful, though she admitted, laughing, that Mr Wickham was the most agreeable man she had ever seen, and that she would not hurry to fall in love.

Wickham's attentions, however, were soon diverted from Elizabeth by Miss King, a young lady who had suddenly inherited ten thousand pounds, and who had been, until then, a person of no interest to him whatever. Elizabeth, who was a clear observer of other people's hearts, saw that her own had been touched only a little, and she wondered at herself for feeling so calm. She told her aunt that she could not blame a poor man for seeking a fortune, though she thought it a pity that his heart should change so quickly.

In London Jane waited impatiently for a visit from Miss Bingley, who had promised to call and who did not appear for nearly a month. When she came, she stayed only a few minutes, spoke of herself and nothing of her brother, and when Jane returned the call in Grosvenor Street she found only the same coldness. Jane, who had always been ready to believe the best of everyone, was at last forced to admit that she had been deceived, and she would no longer be misled by Miss Bingley's kind words.

Charlotte was married very soon afterwards, and she went with her husband to live at the parsonage at Hunsford in Kent, a little house beside the park of Lady Catherine de Bourgh. She wrote cheerfully to Elizabeth of her new home and begged her to visit in the spring, and Elizabeth, though at first unwilling, was at last persuaded. She agreed to travel with Sir William Lucas and his daughter Maria, and before she left she said goodbye to Mr Wickham, who wished her a most agreeable visit.

On the way to Kent the travellers stopped at Gracechurch Street, where Elizabeth found Jane looking well, though a little pale, and where she was happy to see the lively Gardiner household. Her aunt told her that they hoped to take a long tour in the summer, perhaps as far as the Lakes, and Elizabeth, whose heart leapt at the thought, accepted at once. The next day they set out for Hunsford, with Maria chattering and Sir William admiring everything, and Elizabeth, who had never seen Kent, looked from the window with eager expectation.

Elizabeth's journey ended at the gate of the parsonage, where Mr Collins stood waiting to hand the ladies from the carriage, and where Charlotte came out with a smile to welcome her friend. The little house was neat and comfortable, and Mr Collins, who showed it with a pride almost painful to watch, led them through every room and begged them to admire each piece of furniture. Elizabeth, who could not help thinking that he was showing off what he had won, hid her smile as kindly as she could and was glad when Charlotte took her upstairs.

Mr Collins took them next through his garden, which he called one of the chief pleasures of his life, and across every field in the neighbourhood, describing each hedge and tree in such detail that no one else could speak. He could number the fields in every direction and tell how many trees stood in the most distant clump, though no view, he said, could match the sight of Rosings, standing in its park just beyond. Charlotte, who had chosen a quiet back room for her own use, had so arranged matters that her husband was happy in his garden for half the day, and Elizabeth admired her cleverness without envying her.

A day or two after their arrival, Maria Lucas ran into the room with a face of breathless excitement, begging Elizabeth to come to the window to see a sight that she would not describe. It proved to be nothing grander than a little carriage stopped at the garden gate, in which sat Lady Catherine's daughter, Miss de Bourgh, and her companion, while Mr Collins and Charlotte stood outside in deepest respect. Mr Collins was soon in the house again to tell them, with a face full of joy, that Lady Catherine had asked them all to dine at Rosings the next evening.

Mr Collins spent the next day preparing his guests, telling them not to be alarmed by the grandeur of the house, and assuring them that Lady Catherine would not wish them to dress too finely. At Rosings they were led through a magnificent hall and fine rooms, and Sir William was so overcome that he could scarcely bow, while Maria perched in terror on the edge of a chair. Lady Catherine, a tall, large woman with strongly marked features and an air that never forgot rank, sat in state, while her daughter Anne, small, pale and silent, murmured only to her companion.

At dinner Mr Collins carved and ate and praised with delighted energy, and every dish was commended first by him and then by Sir William, while Lady Catherine turned to Elizabeth for a cross-examination. She asked whether Elizabeth played, sang or drew, and when she heard that she did not draw, she called it very strange and blamed her mother for not taking them to town to be taught. When she learned that the five Bennet daughters had grown up without a governess, she cried that she had never heard of such a thing in her life.

Elizabeth answered every question with perfect composure, explaining that those who wished to learn had never lacked the means and that those who chose to be idle certainly might. Lady Catherine then asked whether all five sisters were out at once, and called it very odd that the younger ones should be out before the elder were married. Finally she demanded to know Elizabeth's age, and Elizabeth, smiling, replied that with three younger sisters grown up, her ladyship could hardly expect her to say, and Lady Catherine, astonished at being trifled with, said no more.

Lady Catherine gave her opinion freely to the whole village, settling the quarrels of the poor, and she even called at the parsonage to tell Charlotte how her furniture should be placed. Charlotte listened with perfect patience, and said afterwards, with a smile, that it was a great comfort to have a patroness who took so much interest in her affairs. Elizabeth, who had never met a woman so determined to rule, found her best escape in long walks in the grove beside the park, where she could be alone with her thoughts.

As Easter drew near, Mr Collins announced with great pride that the family at Rosings was to receive a visit from Lady Catherine's nephew, Mr Darcy, who was coming to spend a few weeks with his aunt. Elizabeth, who had not expected anything so disagreeable, was astonished and a little amused, wondering what Mr Darcy would make of finding her in Kent. Charlotte, who had heard something of Mr Darcy at Meryton, said only that the visit would make a pleasant change and that she was eager to see him.

Mr Darcy arrived at Rosings a few days later with his cousin, Colonel Fitzwilliam, the younger son of an earl, and Mr Collins, who had been watching the road for hours, hurried over to pay his respects. He returned in triumph with the news that both gentlemen would call at the parsonage, and the next morning, to everyone's surprise, they did. Colonel Fitzwilliam entered first, and Darcy followed him with his usual reserve, bowing slightly to Mrs Collins and saying very little to Elizabeth.

Colonel Fitzwilliam, a pleasant man of about thirty, was not handsome but was a gentleman in every word and movement, and he talked with such ease that Elizabeth was soon at home with him. Mr Darcy, on the other hand, sat for some time without a word, until at last he politely asked whether the Bennet family were well, and Elizabeth answered that they were. She then asked, with a purpose of her own, whether he had met her sister Jane during her three months in London, and he answered, looking a little confused, that he had never had the good fortune.

On Easter Sunday the parsonage party was invited to dine at Rosings, and when the gentlemen joined the ladies, Colonel Fitzwilliam sat beside Elizabeth and talked with such ease and spirit that she was soon at home. They spoke of Kent and Hertfordshire, of travelling and of staying at home, of new books and of music, and Elizabeth had never been so well entertained in that room. So lively was their talk that it drew the eyes of Mr Darcy, and those of Lady Catherine, who was not in the habit of being left out.

Lady Catherine called across the room, in a voice meant to be heard by all, to ask what they were saying, for she liked to know what was said in her own drawing room. The Colonel, who knew his aunt, answered pleasantly that they were speaking of music, and she replied that she must have her share, since few people in England had more taste or enjoyed it more. She added that she would have been a great proficient herself if she had ever learned, and that Anne, if her health had allowed it, would have played delightfully.

Elizabeth was asked to play after coffee, and she sat down at the instrument, while the Colonel drew up a chair beside her and listened with open pleasure. Mr Darcy, who had been standing at a distance, walked slowly across the room until he stood where he could see her face, and she noticed it and played on with a mischievous smile. “You mean to frighten me, Mr Darcy, by coming so close to hear me,” she said, “but I will not be alarmed, though your sister does play so well.”

Darcy answered that he had no wish to frighten her, and the Colonel, laughing, told Elizabeth that she was in danger of hearing the truth about his cousin. She replied with spirit that at Meryton he would not dance with any lady to whom he had not been introduced, even when young ladies were sitting without partners. Darcy answered gravely that he had not had the pleasure of knowing any lady outside his own party, and that he had not the talent of conversing easily with strangers.

Elizabeth, who felt a playful courage in front of him that she could not explain, added that her fingers did not move like those of the best players, because she had never taken the trouble to practise. Darcy smiled and said that she had employed her time much better, since no one who heard her could think anything wanting. Lady Catherine, who had overheard, cried out that Miss Bennet would never play well unless she practised more, and that she might use the instrument in the housekeeper's room, where she would be in nobody's way.

After that evening the two gentlemen called often at the parsonage, and Charlotte, who watched them closely, saw that the Colonel came for the company, but that Darcy, who sat in long silences, was a puzzle. Elizabeth, who walked each day in the park, met him there again and again, although he never said why, and he asked her odd questions about whether she was happy in Kent. She thought that he must be weary of his own company, but she could not help wondering whether he walked there on purpose.

One afternoon Darcy remarked that Mrs Collins must be happy to be settled so near her family, and Elizabeth answered, with a laugh, that she could hardly call fifty miles an easy distance. Darcy said that fifty miles of good road was little more than half a day's journey, and he drew his chair a little closer to her. Elizabeth replied that she would never have counted distance among the advantages of the match, and Darcy, smiling, said that she could not always have been at Longbourn.

Colonel Fitzwilliam, whom Elizabeth met one morning in the park, joked that a younger son could not marry where he liked, since he was used to comforts and had no fortune to pay for them. Elizabeth asked, smiling, what the usual price of an earl's younger son might be, unless he found a lady with fifty thousand pounds, and the Colonel said that it was a fair guess. He spoke warmly of his cousin, saying that he and Darcy were joint guardians of Miss Darcy and that Darcy took great care of her.

Then, still smiling, the Colonel said that Darcy had lately done a friend the service of saving him from an imprudent marriage, though he did not know the lady's name, only that there were strong objections to her family. Elizabeth, who knew at once that the friend was Mr Bingley, asked what arts had been used to part them, and the Colonel answered that Darcy had not told him. Unable to trust her voice, she walked on in silence, for she saw that Mr Darcy had spoiled her sister's happiness and was the true cause of all that Jane had suffered.

She was so shaken that she pleaded a headache that evening, and when Charlotte and the others set out for Rosings she stayed behind alone. She read again the letters that Jane had written from London, with their gentle complaints and brave pretences, and she could hardly bear to think that a man so proud and cold should have such power over her sister's happiness. She was still burning with anger when the bell rang, and, to her great astonishment, the door opened and Mr Darcy walked into the room.

Mr Darcy asked, in a hurried manner, after her health, and after a few moments of strange silence he began to walk about the room, while Elizabeth watched him with growing astonishment. At last he came towards her, and the words that followed came with an effort that was plain to see. “In vain I have struggled,” he cried, “and it will not do, for you must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.”

Mr Darcy then spoke of her inferior family, of the degradation that a marriage would bring him, and of the long struggle he had fought against his own feelings. Elizabeth, who had begun with pity, grew angrier with every word, for he seemed to think the whole affair a disgrace, and he waited for her answer like a man who expects to be accepted. His voice, his air and his careful speech all told her that he believed he was conferring a great honour, and not asking a favour.

She said that she was sorry for the pain she must give him, but that she could feel no gratitude for sentiments so ill expressed, and that she must refuse him. Darcy, who listened with his eyes fixed on her face and a look of mingled disbelief and mortification, asked in a voice that shook with anger whether that was all the answer he was to have. She replied that she might as well ask why, with so evident a design to insult her, he had told her that he liked her against his will, against his reason and even against his character.

Elizabeth's anger now found its true subject, for she said that no motive could tempt her to accept the man who had ruined, perhaps for ever, the happiness of her beloved sister. She asked whether he could deny that he had separated Mr Bingley from Jane, and had thus exposed one to censure for caprice and the other to the ridicule of disappointed hopes. Darcy answered, with a cold composure that stung her more than anger, that he did not deny it, and that he had been kinder to Bingley than to himself.

She then turned to a second charge, and her voice trembled as she asked how he could defend his treatment of Mr Wickham, whose prospects he had so cruelly destroyed. Darcy changed colour, and said with a bitter smile that she took a very warm interest in that gentleman's concerns. “You have reduced him to his present poverty,” she cried, “and you have kept from him the future that was meant for him by your own father.”

Darcy cried that this was her opinion of him, and then, with a visible effort, he said that perhaps these offences might have been overlooked, had not his honest confession of his scruples hurt her pride. Elizabeth, whose anger now rose to its height, said that from the very first his manners had convinced her of his arrogance, his conceit and his selfish disdain of the feelings of others. She had not known him a month, she told him, before she felt that he was the last man in the world whom she could ever be prevailed on to marry.

Darcy, who had listened with a face of white astonishment, said that he perfectly understood her feelings and had now only to be ashamed of what his own had been. He begged her pardon for taking up so much of her time, wished her health and happiness in a voice that shook a little, and left the house. Elizabeth, whose knees would hardly bear her, sat down and wept for half an hour, bewildered that such a man should have loved her for so many months.

She slept very little that night, and when she woke the whole scene was still before her, so vivid and so unwelcome that she could think of nothing else. Unable to bear the house, she took a long walk in the park, and she had just reached the gate when she saw Mr Darcy coming from the grove. He held out a letter, asked her with great dignity to do him the honour of reading it, and then turned and was soon out of sight.

Elizabeth, with an agitation she could hardly control, broke the seal and read the letter, which began without a word of love and said only that he wrote to answer two charges that she had laid against him. The first was that he had parted Mr Bingley from her sister, because he had believed that Jane felt no special regard, and because her mother and younger sisters had so often shown a total want of propriety. He confessed that he had known of Jane's stay in London and had hidden it from his friend, but he hoped that he had not wounded her sister, since he had acted in good faith.

The second charge, Darcy wrote, concerned Mr Wickham, whom he had known from childhood, the son of his father's steward and a favourite of the old man, who had paid for his schooling and for his years at Cambridge. When the old man died, he had recommended that Wickham should have a good church living if he took orders, but Wickham declared that he no longer wished to be a clergyman and asked for three thousand pounds instead. Darcy gave him the money and ended the connection, and he noted that Wickham had spent it all within a few years, living idly and in expense.

Wickham, Darcy wrote, had come back after the old man's death and demanded the church living that he had given up, and when he was refused, he had become Darcy's bitter enemy. But the worst of the story belonged to the last summer, when Georgiana, only fifteen, went to Ramsgate with a lady named Mrs Younge, and Wickham followed them by design and persuaded her that she was in love. Darcy, who arrived unexpectedly a day or two before the planned elopement, learned the whole from his sister, who could not bear to grieve a brother she looked up to as a father.

The letter ended with the statement that Wickham's chief object was Georgiana's fortune of thirty thousand pounds, and that Colonel Fitzwilliam, who knew the whole affair, could confirm every word. Elizabeth, who at first refused to believe a syllable, read on with a feeling close to horror, and more than once she declared that it must be false. But on reading it again, calmly, she remembered that Wickham had told his story to a stranger, that he had offered no proof, and that nobody in Meryton had known him before the regiment came.

Every lingering struggle in his favour grew fainter and fainter, and she grew absolutely ashamed of herself, for she saw that she had been blind, partial, prejudiced and absurd. She remembered his attentions to Miss King, which now seemed mercenary, and the ease with which he had told a stranger of wrongs that no gentleman should have spread. “How despicably I have acted,” she cried, “I who have prided myself on my discernment, for vanity, not love, has been my folly, and until this moment I never knew myself!”

She walked for two hours, lost in thought, and returned to the parsonage so tired and so changed that she could hardly bear the thought of company. Charlotte told her that Mr Darcy and Colonel Fitzwilliam had called during her absence, and that the Colonel had waited an hour in the hope of her return, to say goodbye. Elizabeth could only pretend to regret it, for her mind was fixed on the letter, which she read again and again until she knew every line by heart.

That evening at Rosings was very dull, for the two nephews had gone, and Lady Catherine, in a poor humour, complained that the house was empty. She begged Elizabeth to stay two weeks longer, and when Elizabeth explained that her aunt expected her in London, she asked why she should not stay another month. Elizabeth, who guessed that the lady wished only for company, answered with perfect politeness that she was sorry to disappoint her, but that she had already given her word.

On the last morning Lady Catherine fussed over the journey, saying that two young women must never travel alone, and that Mrs Collins must send a servant with them. Mr Collins made a long speech of thanks for the honour of Elizabeth's visit, and assured her that, if Hunsford could offer little society, Lady Catherine's condescension was some compensation. Elizabeth kissed Charlotte at the door and saw that her friend, who had chosen her fate, bore it with a quiet content, though she was sorry to leave her to such a husband.

The journey to London was quick, and in Gracechurch Street Elizabeth found Jane looking well, though a little thinner and quieter than before, and she was greeted by her young cousins with delight.
