She had much to tell her sister, but she resolved to say nothing yet of the proposal, since it would mean telling how Mr Darcy had parted Jane from Mr Bingley. For the present she kept the secret, and she busied herself with the shops and the children until it was time to go home to Hertfordshire.

On the road home, at an inn near Longbourn, the sisters found Kitty and Lydia watching from the window of the dining room, where they had laid out a cold luncheon of salad and cucumber and cold meat. Lydia, who was delighted to see them, held up a new bonnet that she had bought, saying that it was very ugly but that she had bought it because it was cheap and might do when trimmed. She declared that the regiment was to leave Meryton in a few weeks, and that she should be wretched without the officers, who were going to camp at Brighton.

At Longbourn Lydia, who could talk of nothing but the officers, told her sisters that Mrs Forster, the young wife of the Colonel, had asked her to go with her to Brighton. The regiment was to move there for the summer, Lydia explained, and she would stay for the whole season, with the balls and the camp and the sea-bathing that she thought the finest things in the world. Kitty, who had not been asked, cried with envy, while Mrs Bennet declared that nothing could be more delightful for the family.

Elizabeth, who saw only disgrace in such a plan, begged her father in private not to let Lydia go, for she was wild, ignorant and vain, and Brighton was full of officers. Mr Bennet answered mildly that Lydia would never be easy until she had made a fool of herself in some public place, and that she could hardly do it more cheaply than now. Elizabeth, seeing that her father would not listen, gave up the argument with a sigh, and Lydia, in raptures, began to pack her trunks.

Elizabeth told Jane the story of the proposal at Hunsford, and Jane, who could hardly believe that a man so reserved could have felt so strongly, was astonished, and her sympathy was divided between her sister and Mr Darcy. When Elizabeth went on to what she had learned of Wickham, Jane, whose gentle heart refused to think any man so wicked, was deeply troubled, and begged to be allowed to believe that there had been some mistake. The sisters agreed to tell the story to no one, since Wickham would soon leave, and Elizabeth, who could not bear to cause her sister more pain, said nothing of Mr Bingley.

The regiment was preparing to leave Meryton, and while the ladies of the neighbourhood lamented, Elizabeth, who saw it go with relief, spoke to Mr Wickham for the last time at a dinner at Colonel Forster's. When he asked about Kent, she said that she had met Mr Darcy there and thought him much improved, and she added, with a look he could not mistake, that she knew the truth about the living. He looked alarmed and confused, but he recovered with a laugh, and they parted with the smiles of two people who understand each other and do not wish to say so.

The Gardiners arrived at Longbourn in July, as they had promised, and Elizabeth, who needed a change more than anyone knew, prepared joyfully to travel with them for several weeks. But Mr Gardiner's business, which could not be left for so long, obliged them to shorten the tour, and instead of the Lakes they were to go no further than Derbyshire. Mrs Gardiner, who had lived there as a girl, was delighted with the change, and Elizabeth, who had little reason to dislike the county except for one name, said nothing against it.

They travelled by easy stages through the most beautiful country in England, admiring the sights that every tourist admires, and at last they came to Lambton, the little town where Mrs Gardiner had spent her youth. There Mrs Gardiner confessed that she wished to see Pemberley, the famous house five miles away, and she urged her niece to come, since it seemed a pity to be so near and not go. Elizabeth, who blushed at the very name, agreed only after the chambermaid at the inn assured her that the family was away, and she began to look forward to the visit with curiosity and dread.

The park was large and varied, and they drove for some time through beautiful woods, until the carriage reached a rise where the trees ended and Pemberley House appeared across the valley. It was a large, handsome house of stone, standing on rising ground with a ridge of wooded hills behind it, and in front a stream flowed that looked natural and yet grand. Elizabeth, who had never seen a place where nature had done more, or where beauty had been so little spoiled by false taste, felt that to be mistress of Pemberley might be something.

They were admitted by the housekeeper, Mrs Reynolds, a respectable elderly woman, much less fine and much more civil than Elizabeth had expected, who led them through rooms that were elegant without being showy. Elizabeth admired every room and every view from every window, and she thought that she might have been mistress of it all, welcoming her uncle and aunt as guests, until she remembered with a start that it could never be. Among the little portraits on a table Mrs Reynolds pointed to Mr Wickham and said sadly that he had gone into the army, but that she feared he had turned out very wild.

Mrs Reynolds spoke of her master with the warmth of long affection, saying that he was the best landlord and the best master that ever lived, not like the wild young men who thought only of themselves. She had known him since he was four years old, she said, and she had never had a cross word from him, for he had always been the sweetest-tempered, most generous-hearted boy in the world. Elizabeth, listening with growing astonishment, could hardly believe that this was the man whom she had thought so proud, and her uncle, smiling, remarked that such praise from a servant was worth more than any other.

They passed next into the long gallery, where hung many family portraits, and Elizabeth walked slowly along the wall in search of the one face that she would know. At last she found it, and she saw a striking likeness of Mr Darcy, with a smile such as she remembered seeing when he had looked at her. She stood several minutes before the picture in earnest thought, and she felt for the first time a warm regard for the man himself, remembering how much good he did and how much happiness was in his power.

When they had seen the rooms, the party walked out across the lawn toward the river, and at that moment the owner himself appeared on the road from the stables, so near that they could not avoid him. Their eyes met, and the cheeks of both were overspread with a deep blush, and for a moment he seemed unable to move from surprise. Then, recovering, he came forward and spoke to Elizabeth, if not in terms of perfect composure, at least of perfect civility, and he asked after her family, while she, in confusion, hardly knew what she answered.

He explained that he had arrived a day earlier than expected, and he apologised, with an awkwardness that Elizabeth had never seen in him, for any trouble that his coming might cause. When Elizabeth, in some alarm, introduced her aunt and uncle, he was so cordial and attentive to them, whom she had feared he would despise, that all three were astonished. Before they parted he invited Mr Gardiner to fish in his river whenever he pleased and offered to lend him tackle, and Mr Gardiner, who had not expected such kindness, accepted with pleasure.

Before they parted, Darcy asked Elizabeth with obvious hesitation whether he might introduce his sister to her, a mark of respect so unexpected that she could only give a flustered consent. When he had gone, her uncle and aunt, who had expected a haughty man and found an obliging one, wondered aloud what had caused such a change. Mrs Gardiner, who thought she saw a reason in his attention to her niece, gave Elizabeth a significant look, and Elizabeth, colouring, said only that she had never known him so polite.

The next morning Darcy arrived at the inn with his sister, who was tall, shy and gentle, with a face full of sense and good humour and manners free from all pride. Elizabeth, who had expected the fine airs of a great lady, saw only a girl so timid that she could hardly speak, and she remembered with a pang how cruelly such a heart had been used. Georgiana, who had often heard her brother speak of Miss Bennet, looked at her with open admiration, and the two were soon talking more easily than either had expected.

While they were talking, a quick step was heard on the stairs, and Mr Bingley appeared, with a face of such open pleasure at seeing Elizabeth that she could not doubt the warmth of his feelings. He spoke of Netherfield, and he remembered, to her great surprise, the exact day on which they had last met, the twenty-sixth of November, when they had all been dancing together. He asked, with a look that said more than his words, whether all her sisters were at Longbourn, and Elizabeth, who saw that Jane was still in his thoughts, answered with gladness she tried to hide.

On the day appointed Elizabeth and the Gardiners called at Pemberley, where Georgiana received them kindly, but where Miss Bingley and Mrs Hurst offered a chilly civility in place of welcome. Miss Bingley, who had resolved to put Elizabeth out of countenance, asked whether the militia had left Meryton, and what a loss it must be to her family, though she dared not name Mr Wickham in Darcy's presence. Elizabeth answered calmly and briefly, and betrayed nothing, though Georgiana, who understood the hint, blushed painfully and could not lift her eyes.

When Elizabeth had gone, Miss Bingley began at once to criticise her, declaring that she was grown so brown and coarse that she and her sister would hardly have known her again. She added that her features were not good, that her nose wanted character, and that her eyes, which some called fine, were nothing out of the ordinary. Darcy, who had listened with a growing frown, answered coldly that he saw no change in her except a sunburn from summer travel, and that he had long thought her one of the handsomest women of his acquaintance.

Elizabeth, who returned to the inn in a state of grateful wonder, found there two letters from Jane, which should have reached her sooner but had been sent first to the wrong place. The first, written several days earlier, began calmly with local news, but a few lines further it grew hurried and strange, and Jane wrote that something most serious had happened. An express had come at midnight from Colonel Forster to say that Lydia had gone off to Scotland with one of his officers, and Jane, trembling, confessed that the officer was Wickham.

The second letter, written a day later, was shorter and more anxious, for it said that Colonel Forster had traced the runaways as far as London but no further. A hint dropped by Mr Denny suggested that Wickham had never meant to go to Scotland or to marry Lydia at all, and Mr Bennet had gone to London with the Colonel to search for her. Jane begged Elizabeth and her uncle to come home at once, for her mother was ill, her father needed help, and she herself could give comfort to no one.

Elizabeth, who had hurried out to find her uncle, was met by Mr Darcy, who saw her pale face and asked, in a tone of deep concern, what had happened. She told him that her youngest sister had eloped with Mr Wickham, that he knew him too well to doubt the rest, and that if only she had told what she knew, it might never have happened. Darcy, who listened in shocked silence, said that he was grieved indeed, paced the room with a gloomy face, and went away, leaving her sure that she had lost his regard for ever.

Left alone, Elizabeth felt, as never before, how honestly she could have loved him now that all hope was gone, and she saw that her sister's disgrace must end any thought he had of her. She reproached herself bitterly for having kept silent about Wickham, since she had never imagined that he could ruin a girl who had no money to tempt him. Her uncle and aunt, who came in pale with alarm, heard the news with horror, and it was agreed that they must leave for Longbourn without delay.

They travelled home as fast as the horses would go, and Mr Gardiner, who was shocked but not without hope, said that Wickham could hardly be so foolish as to ruin a girl who was under his colonel's protection. Elizabeth, who knew what he did not, answered that she feared the worst, but she said no more of his history, for she wished only to reach her family. At Longbourn Jane met her at the door with a face that spoke of sleepless nights, while Mrs Bennet lay upstairs, weeping and blaming everyone but herself.

Jane told her sister all that was known: that Lydia had left a few lines for Mrs Forster saying she was going to Gretna Green, and that Wickham, it now appeared, owed large sums to the shopkeepers of Meryton. Kitty, pale and tearful, confessed that she had known for some time that Lydia was in love with Wickham, though a promise had bound her to silence. Elizabeth, who now saw only what Wickham really was, felt her shame turn into a cold anger at the thought of how many people his charm had deceived.

Mrs Bennet kept to her room, where she wept and blamed Colonel Forster, and cried that Mr Bennet would be killed in a duel and that they would all be turned out of doors. The house was in confusion, for Mr Bennet had gone to London with the Colonel, and Mary lectured her sisters on the danger of losing a good name while the servants whispered in corners. Mr Gardiner, who had gone on to London to help his brother-in-law, wrote that he would do all that a brother could, and asked to be told of any news.

After some days Mr Bennet returned from London, having found no trace of the runaways, and his daughters were shocked to see how old and tired and ashamed he looked. “Let me once in my life feel how much I have been to blame,” he said, when Elizabeth tried to comfort him, “for I am not afraid of being overpowered by it, and it will pass away soon enough.” He added, with a faint return of his old humour, that Kitty should never go out until she could prove that she had spent ten minutes of every day in a rational manner.

Soon afterwards a letter arrived from Mr Collins, who wrote in his most solemn style that he and Charlotte sincerely sympathised with the family in a distress of the bitterest kind. He declared that the death of Lydia would have been a blessing in comparison with such a disgrace, and he suggested that it had no doubt come of too much indulgence. He advised Mr Bennet to cast off his unworthy child for ever, and Mr Bennet, who read the whole aloud with a bitter smile, wondered what Lady Catherine would say.

At last a letter arrived from Mr Gardiner, written in haste, to say that he had found the runaways in London, and that Wickham, to everyone's astonishment, was willing to marry Lydia. The terms were modest, he wrote: Lydia was to have a hundred pounds a year, and an equal share of the five thousand pounds to be divided among the daughters after her parents' deaths. Mr Bennet, who read the letter twice with growing wonder, said that Wickham could not be such a fool as to take Lydia on such terms, and that someone must have been paid.

Mr Bennet thought it most unlikely that Wickham would take a girl without a fortune for so little, and he guessed that his brother-in-law had paid a great deal more than he said. He said that he would not rest until he knew how much Gardiner had done and how it could be repaid, for it was a debt of the kind that lasts a lifetime. Elizabeth and Jane, who were happy and ashamed at once, agreed that the family could never repay their uncle's goodness, and they hurried to tell their mother the news.

Mrs Bennet, who had been in despair for a week, was transported with joy at the news, and she thought only of seeing her youngest daughter a wife at sixteen, with a fine house and fine clothes. She began at once to name the muslins that Lydia should order and begged her husband to pay, but Mr Bennet answered that he would not advance one guinea for wedding clothes. Mrs Bennet was more distressed at the thought of Lydia being married without a new gown than at the shame of her elopement.

Elizabeth, meanwhile, bitterly regretted that she had ever told Mr Darcy of her sister's disgrace, for she now felt, with a pain that surprised her, how much she wanted his good opinion. Mr Gardiner wrote that Wickham had found a place in a regular regiment in the north of England, far from his debts, and that he and Lydia wished to visit Longbourn on their way. Mr Bennet, who at first refused to see them, was persuaded by Jane and Elizabeth, who feared that Lydia's chance of being received anywhere would depend on how her own family treated her.

Lydia and Wickham arrived at Longbourn, and when the carriage stopped, Mrs Bennet smiled and held out her arms, while her husband, who had never looked so grave, hardly nodded. Lydia, untamed, unabashed and noisy, jumped from the carriage and kissed her mother and her sisters in turn, while Wickham, as easy and charming as ever, shook hands with the whole family and wished them joy. Elizabeth, who had not thought that any man could have so much assurance, could hardly bear to look at him, and Jane, whose cheeks had turned crimson, kept her eyes on the floor.

Lydia, in the highest spirits, held up her hand to show her ring, and told Jane that she must give up her place at the table and go lower, because she herself was now a married woman. She described her wedding in loud and breathless detail, and Mrs Bennet, who sat beaming at her side, declared that she had never looked so well. Elizabeth, who had hoped to see some sign of shame and found only pride, wished that she could sink into the ground.

Lydia, chattering about her wedding with her usual lack of reserve, said all at once that Mr Darcy had been there, and then she clapped a hand to her mouth, for she had promised to say nothing. Elizabeth, whose heart leapt at the name, said that if it was meant to be a secret, she would not ask another word. But she was left in such astonishment that she could think of nothing else, and she wondered why a man who despised her family should have gone to such a wedding.

Elizabeth could not rest until she had written to her aunt, begging her to explain, if it were not contrary to the secret, how Mr Darcy had come to be present at so private a ceremony. She turned the matter over a hundred times, and her first thought, which she tried to dismiss as vanity, was that he had done it for her sake. But she could not believe that a man so proud would take such trouble for a family that she had told him she despised.

Wickham, who found himself walking with Elizabeth on the day before they left, asked with his old easy air whether she had liked Pemberley, and she replied that she had seen it and had liked it very much. She added that she had heard from a source as good as his own that the church living had been left to him only on conditions, and Wickham, changing colour, said that he remembered something of the kind. “We are brother and sister now, Mr Wickham,” she said, with gentle firmness, “so let us not quarrel about the past, and I hope that in future we shall always be of one mind.”

Wickham and Lydia left a few days later for Newcastle, where his new regiment was stationed, and Lydia, as gay and loud as ever, kissed her sisters and told them to find husbands for themselves. Mrs Bennet cried that it was the hardest thing in the world to part with children, and she sank into low spirits for several weeks. Mr Bennet, who had been much entertained by his new son-in-law, remarked that Wickham simpered and smirked and made love to them all, and that he was prodigiously proud of him.

A letter from Mrs Gardiner at last brought the answer, and Elizabeth, who took it into the shrubbery to read alone, learned that Darcy had found the runaways through Mrs Younge, and had seen both of them in London. When Lydia would not leave Wickham, Darcy had paid all his debts, added to Lydia's small fortune, and bought his place in the army, insisting that the whole cost should be his. His only reason, wrote Mrs Gardiner, was that he blamed his own pride for not making Wickham's character known, and he had begged that the secret should be kept.

Elizabeth read the letter over and over, and she was proud and grateful and ashamed all at once, for she could hardly bear to think that she owed to Darcy the very honour of her family. She remembered the cold words she had spoken at Hunsford, and she saw that he had gone to such lengths for her when he must have believed that all hope of her was gone. She had never honoured him so much as now, and she would have given anything for the power to thank him, but she saw no chance of ever meeting him again.

About this time news reached Longbourn that drove Lydia from every mind: Mrs Nicholls, the housekeeper at Netherfield, had been told to prepare for her master, who was to come down within a few days. Mr Bennet declared that he would not call on the young man a second time, but his wife begged and scolded until he sighed that he would call when he must. Jane, who had grown pale at the news, told Elizabeth that she was glad he was coming, and that she wished only to meet him as a friend.

When the gentlemen at last rode over, Jane looked pale but composed, while Elizabeth, who hardly dared to raise her eyes, saw that Darcy had come with Bingley, looking as grave as ever. Mrs Bennet, who received Mr Bingley with the warmest civility, was so cold and so nearly rude to Mr Darcy that Elizabeth, who knew what she owed him, was ready to cry with shame. He asked after Mr and Mrs Gardiner with some effort, said little more, and sat for the rest of the visit looking not at her but at the floor.

As the visit ended, Mrs Bennet, who could never be content with a little happiness, reminded Mr Bingley that he owed her a family dinner, which he had promised when he went to town the winter before. Bingley, looking a little confused, said that business had prevented him, but that he would gladly name any day, and Tuesday was fixed on the spot. Elizabeth, who had barely looked at Darcy, wondered at his gravity and silence, and thought with a heavy heart that he had come only out of friendship for Bingley and had no thought of her at all.

On Tuesday the two gentlemen came punctually, and Elizabeth, who watched with eager eyes, saw that Bingley sat next to Jane, but that Darcy was placed at a distance from her, close to her mother. He was so quiet that he hardly spoke, and Elizabeth, who felt more and more unhappy, told herself that if he did not come to her after dinner, she would give him up for ever. When the ladies went to the drawing room, she waited with a heavy heart for the gentlemen, certain that the evening would show whether he cared for her at all.

When the gentlemen joined the ladies, Elizabeth watched Mr Darcy enter with a hope that she could hardly bear, and she saw him take a chair at a distance, near her mother's table, with his cup of coffee. Jane and Bingley, who sat side by side, were so absorbed in each other that they seemed to forget everyone else, while Elizabeth, who poured out the coffee, grew more anxious as the minutes passed. The evening ended without a word between them, and Elizabeth, who had hoped for so much, went to her room feeling that she had been more foolish than anyone could know.

Darcy went to London the next morning, to be absent for some time, but Bingley, who had never been in better spirits, came to Longbourn again as soon as he was able. Mrs Bennet, who could see how matters stood, found every kind of excuse for sending her other daughters out of the room, so that Jane and Bingley might have time to themselves. Elizabeth, who understood her mother's manoeuvres and wished the lovers well, was soon out of the room herself, and she left them in a long and whispering conversation.

That evening Bingley asked Jane to marry him, and she said yes, with tears of joy that she could not hide. She ran to find her mother, and then to Elizabeth, whom she embraced and told that she was the happiest creature in the world, and that she did not deserve it. Elizabeth, who felt more happiness than she could express, kissed her again and again, and said that nobody in the world deserved such joy more.

Bingley, who was impatient, spoke to Mr Bennet at once and received a kind and cheerful permission, for Mr Bennet liked the young man and had long wished that Jane might be happy. Mrs Bennet, who was beside herself with delight, declared that she had always known it would be so, that Jane was too beautiful to be overlooked, and that Bingley was the most charming man in England. Within a few days he was the dearest of her sons-in-law, and her only regret was that she could not tell Lady Lucas fast enough.

A few days later, early in the morning, the family was at breakfast when the noise of a carriage drew them to the window, and they saw a chaise and four driving up to the door, which no one recognised. Mrs Bennet and Kitty were still guessing who it might be when the door was thrown open, and Elizabeth, to her astonishment, saw Lady Catherine de Bourgh walk in. Her ladyship, who looked more haughty than ever, answered Mrs Bennet's greeting with a slight nod, sat down without a word, and asked Elizabeth whether she would walk with her in the garden.

When they were alone in the little wilderness beside the lawn, Lady Catherine announced in a voice that shook with anger that she was not to be trifled with, and that she would be sincere. A report of an alarming nature, she said, had reached her two days before, that Jane was to be well married and that Elizabeth would soon marry her own nephew, Mr Darcy. Though she knew it must be a scandalous falsehood, she had driven all that way to insist that it should be contradicted at once.

Elizabeth answered, with cold surprise, that if her ladyship thought the report impossible, she wondered why she had taken the trouble of coming so far. When Lady Catherine demanded to know whether Mr Darcy had made her an offer, Elizabeth replied that her ladyship had called it impossible, and that she would not answer questions put in such a manner. Lady Catherine declared that the match could never take place, since Mr Darcy was engaged to her own daughter and the two had been intended for each other from the cradle.

Elizabeth said that she would certainly not be kept from marrying him merely by the knowledge that his mother and aunt had wished him to marry Miss de Bourgh. Lady Catherine cried that honour and prudence forbade it, and she spoke with scorn of Elizabeth's low relations and of the shame of Lydia's elopement. “He is a gentleman, and I am a gentleman's daughter,” said Elizabeth, rising in anger, “so far we are equal.”

Lady Catherine demanded to know whether she was engaged to Mr Darcy, and when Elizabeth, after a moment, said that she was not, she asked for a promise that she never would be, which Elizabeth firmly refused. “I am only resolved,” said Elizabeth, “to act in that manner which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness, and you have no right to concern yourself in my affairs.” Lady Catherine, who said that she took no leave of her and sent no compliments to her mother, got into her carriage in a fury and drove away.

Elizabeth, who stood for some time after the carriage had gone, was more disturbed than she wished to show, and she wondered what Mr Darcy would do when his aunt told him of her visit. A few days later her father called her into the library, where he held up a letter from Mr Collins, which congratulated him on Jane's engagement and added a hint that a still more illustrious match was expected for Elizabeth. “It is delightfully absurd,” he said, laughing, “for Mr Darcy never looks at you, and you dislike him so very much.”

A few days later Darcy returned with Bingley, who proposed that the whole party should walk out, and though Mrs Bennet and Mary begged to be excused, Kitty, Jane and Elizabeth agreed gladly. Jane and Bingley soon fell behind, and Kitty went on to call on Maria Lucas, so that Elizabeth and Darcy were left to walk alone, each in a silence that grew heavier with every step. At last Elizabeth, summoning all her courage at once, resolved to say what she had long wished to say.

“I am a very selfish creature, Mr Darcy,” she said, “but I can no longer help thanking you for your extraordinary kindness to my poor sister.” She explained that Lydia's thoughtlessness had first betrayed to her what he had done, and that she thanked him in the name of all her family. Darcy, who was exceedingly surprised, said that he was sorry she had ever been told, and that he had not thought Mrs Gardiner so little to be trusted.

“You must not blame my aunt,” said Elizabeth, “for it was Lydia who first betrayed you, and I could not rest until I knew the particulars.” “If you will thank me,” he answered, “let it be for yourself alone, for I believe that I thought only of you, and your family owe me nothing.” After a pause he added that if her feelings were still what they had been in April she must say so at once, for his own were unchanged, but a word would silence him for ever.

Elizabeth, feeling the anxiety of his situation, forced herself to speak at last, and she gave him to understand, though not fluently, that her feelings had changed so much since April that she heard him with gratitude and pleasure. The happiness that her answer gave was such as he had probably never felt before, and he spoke as warmly as a man violently in love can be supposed to do. They walked on without knowing in which direction, for there was too much to be thought, and felt, and said, to leave any attention for other things.

Darcy told her, as they walked, that he had learned of her refusal from his aunt herself, who had stopped in London to tell him every particular of her visit, with bitter emphasis on Elizabeth's obstinacy. Far from discouraging him, the tale had taught him to hope, for he knew her well enough to be certain that, if she had been truly decided against him, she would have said so openly. Elizabeth, laughing and colouring, answered that he knew her frankness well, since after abusing him so abominably to his face she could have no scruple in abusing him to all his relations.

Darcy spoke with deep feeling of his words at Hunsford, which he called unpardonable, and of her reproof, which had tortured him for months before he was reasonable enough to allow its justice. Elizabeth begged him not to repeat what she had said, for she had long been ashamed of it, and she added that the conduct of neither would bear a strict examination, though both had improved in civility since. “You taught me a lesson, hard at first but most advantageous,” he said, “for I came to you without a doubt of my reception, and you showed me how little my pretensions were worth.”

She asked him, smiling, when he had begun to love her, and he said that he could not fix the hour or the look, for he was in the middle before he knew that he had begun. When she asked whether he had admired her for her impertinence, he answered that it was for the liveliness of her mind, and that his manners to her had always been at best uncivil. He told her, too, that he had confessed his mistake to Bingley, who had forgiven him at once and gone to find his answer, for he had never ceased to love Jane.

When Elizabeth came home, Jane, who was alone with her, asked where on earth she had been walking, and Elizabeth, blushing and smiling, said at last that she was engaged to Mr Darcy. Jane, who had so long known that her sister hated him, cried that she was joking, that it was quite impossible, and that she would not be deceived. Elizabeth, a little hurt, insisted that it was the plain truth, and that nothing less could have made her say it.

Convinced at last, Jane embraced her with a joy that could find no words, and asked how long she had loved him, to which Elizabeth answered, laughing, that it had begun when she first saw his grounds at Pemberley. That night Mr Bennet, who had been spoken to by Darcy in the library, called Elizabeth to him and asked whether she was out of her senses to accept a man whom she had always hated. Elizabeth assured him that she loved Darcy, and told him all that he had done for the family, until her father said that he could not have parted with her to anyone less worthy.

Mr Bennet, who learned that it was Darcy and not Mr Gardiner who had settled Lydia's affairs, said that it was so much the better, since it would save him a world of trouble and economy. He added, laughing, that he would offer to pay Darcy the next day, and that the young man would rave about his love, and the matter would be settled. When Elizabeth told her mother, Mrs Bennet sat for a long time without a syllable, and then she cried that Mr Darcy had ten thousand a year, and very likely more, which was as good as a lord.

Mrs Bennet's rapture was such that she could hardly sit still, yet in Darcy's presence she was so much in awe of him that she scarcely dared to speak, and she answered him with a respect that astonished her husband. Mr Bennet, who liked his future son-in-law more than he had expected, remarked that he admired all three of his sons-in-law highly, though Wickham was perhaps his favourite. Elizabeth, who saw how his mild irony hid a real kindness, was glad that her father approved, and she felt her last doubts melt away.

Elizabeth wrote at once to her aunt, and Mrs Gardiner replied in a letter full of joy, saying that she had hoped for such an end ever since Pemberley, and that she could not say how delighted she was. A letter also came from Mr Collins, who congratulated Mr Bennet in his most ceremonious style, but warned him that Lady Catherine would be very displeased, and advised him to prevent the match. Charlotte added a few warm lines of her own, and Elizabeth, who had half forgotten her old displeasure with her friend, was glad of them.

Elizabeth and Darcy talked for hours of all that had passed, and she teased him, with the new freedom that happiness gave her, for looking so cold when he first came to Longbourn and again at dinner. He answered that she had been grave and silent and had given him no encouragement, and that he had been embarrassed, and she replied that so had she, and that he might have talked more. “A man who had felt less might have found it easier,” he said with a smile.

Darcy, who had written at once to tell his aunt of the engagement, received in return a letter so abusive, especially of Elizabeth, that for some time all intercourse between them was at an end. Elizabeth read it with a smile and a little sadness, and said that she could not bear to be the cause of a quarrel in his family, and that in time he must forgive his aunt. Georgiana, who had been told by her brother in a long and affectionate letter, replied with a warmth that delighted Elizabeth, saying that she had always wished for a sister and could hardly express her pleasure.

Miss Bingley was deeply mortified by Darcy's marriage, but she thought it wise to keep her right to visit Pemberley, and so she dropped her resentment and wrote a congratulation full of affection. Elizabeth, who saw through every sweet phrase, answered with such perfect politeness that Miss Bingley could not complain, and she felt, to her surprise, almost a kind of pity for her. The Hursts followed their sister's example, and Mr Hurst was heard to say that the dinners at Pemberley were the best he had ever eaten.

Happy for all her motherly feelings was the day on which Mrs Bennet got rid of her two most deserving daughters, for Jane and Elizabeth were married together in the little church at Longbourn. Mr Bennet, who gave each of them away with a gravity that did not quite hide his feeling, was seen to wipe his eyes, and the Gardiners, who had come from London, wept without shame. Mrs Bennet, who was so proud that she could hardly stand still, visited her neighbours afterwards to talk of Mrs Bingley and Mrs Darcy, and she liked the second name best.

When the carriage reached the rise where the woods end, Elizabeth saw the great house in its valley, no longer a place admired by a stranger, but the home that she would share for the rest of her life. Mrs Reynolds, who waited in the hall with tears in her eyes, welcomed her so warmly that Elizabeth, remembering all that the housekeeper had said of her master, could not help smiling at her husband. Georgiana, who now had the sister she had always wished for, ran to meet her, and was soon astonished to hear Elizabeth tease her brother with a freedom that she had never dared to use.

Mr Bingley and Jane stayed at Netherfield for only a year, since it was too near her mother, and then he bought an estate near Derbyshire, so that the sisters lived within thirty miles. Kitty, to her great advantage, spent most of her time with her two elder sisters, and in such society, removed from Lydia's example, she became less irritable, less ignorant and less foolish. Mr Bennet, who missed his second daughter exceedingly, delighted in visiting Pemberley, especially when he was least expected, while Mrs Bennet remained occasionally nervous and invariably silly, but never tired of describing the glories of her daughters' homes.

As for Wickham and Lydia, their characters did not change, and Lydia often wrote to ask Elizabeth for money, which she received, a little at a time, though never as much as she wished. Lady Catherine, who had been extremely indignant at the marriage, was at length persuaded by Elizabeth to be reconciled to her nephew, and her anger gave way to her curiosity to see how his wife behaved. She condescended at last to call at Pemberley, in spite of the pollution that its woods had received from the presence of such a mistress and the visits of her uncle and aunt from the city.

With the Gardiners, Darcy and Elizabeth were always on the most intimate terms, for they both loved them, and they never forgot that it was a journey into Derbyshire that had united them. Whenever Pemberley rang with laughter and the music of Georgiana's piano, they remembered the Meryton ball and the three muddy miles, and smiled at how long it had taken two clever people to see each other clearly. And so the proud man who had once found a young woman only tolerable, and the lively girl who had sworn to dislike him for life, lived on together in a happiness that no later quarrel ever spoiled.
